questions.direct_answer: MongoDB stores data as flexible JSON-like BSON documents within collections, allowing nested structures and arrays without a fixed schema. Relational databases store data in rigid tables with rows and columns, enforcing a schema and using foreign keys for relationships. sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Embed for co-accessed data; reference for shared or large data** — order items embedded in the order document read in one query; shared products referenced to avoid duplicating data across thousands of orders
- **Embedded arrays must be bounded** — MongoDB's 16MB document limit and performance degrade with unbounded embedded arrays; use referencing when the related collection grows without limit
- **`$lookup` for server-side joins on referenced data** — equivalent to a SQL LEFT JOIN; works on non-sharded collections; avoid in the inner loop of a sharded aggregation
- **Schema flexibility requires application-level validation** — missing fields and type mismatches don't raise database errors; use `$jsonSchema` validators or application-layer guards to enforce structure
- **Design schemas around access patterns, not normalization** — MongoDB benefits from query-driven design; start with how the application reads data, then decide what to embed vs reference

sections.title: How to Explain Document Model vs Relational Model
sections.content:
MongoDB stores data as flexible JSON-like BSON documents in collections, where related data can be nested as sub-documents rather than split across multiple tables. The key design question is whether to embed or reference — and the answer comes from your read patterns.

**The fundamental difference**
- In a relational database, a single order might span four tables — `orders`, `order_items`, `customers`, `products` — requiring JOINs to reconstruct; in MongoDB, the order document can contain all its items as an embedded array, making a single document read return everything the application needs
- Embedding is fast for reads because no JOIN equivalent is needed; referencing is necessary when the related data is large, changes frequently, or is shared across many documents

**When to embed**
- Embed when the related data is always accessed together with the parent — order items are always fetched with the order; embedding them avoids a second query
- Embed when the related data is bounded in size — an order might have 1-50 items; embedding a potentially unbounded collection creates documents that grow without limit
- MongoDB documents are limited to 16MB; deeply embedded arrays that grow indefinitely will hit this limit

**When to reference**
- Reference when the related entity is shared — a product referenced by thousands of orders; embedding a copy in every order duplicates data and makes product updates require touching every order document
- Reference when the related data is large or needs independent querying — user comments on a post might number in the thousands; embedding them makes the post document unwieldy
- Use `$lookup` in the aggregation pipeline to join referenced documents server-side, similar to a SQL JOIN

**Schema flexibility trade-off**
- MongoDB's flexible schema allows different documents in the same collection to have different fields — useful for schema evolution and sparse attributes; the trade-off is that the application must handle missing fields and type variations that a relational schema would reject at the database level

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
Embedding means storing related data as a sub-document or array within the parent document, which makes reads fast but can lead to large documents and update anomalies.

Referencing stores related data in a separate collection and links via an ID, similar to a foreign key, keeping documents small but requiring $lookup or application-level joins.

questions.question: Explain the different types of indexes in MongoDB — compound, sparse, and TTL — and how you use them in a Spring Boot application.
questions.title: Indexing in MongoDB: Compound, Sparse, and TTL Indexes
questions.direct_answer: MongoDB supports several index types beyond the default single-field index. A compound index covers multiple fields and supports sorting. A sparse index only indexes documents that contain the indexed field, saving space for optional fields. A TTL (Time-To-Live) index automatically deletes documents after a specified duration, ideal for session or log data. In Spring Boot you declare indexes via @Indexed, @CompoundIndex, and @Document annotations or programmatically through MongoTemplate.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Compound index left-prefix rule** — `{ user_id: 1, status: 1 }` cannot serve `{ status: ?}` alone; the leading field must appear in the query filter
- **Sparse index for optional fields** — excludes documents missing the indexed field; prevents the index from growing with null entries for a field that only a fraction of documents have
- **TTL index for automatic document expiry** — `expireAfterSeconds` on a date field auto-deletes documents after the duration; the TTL monitor runs every 60s so expiry is approximate
- **Multikey index for array fields** — MongoDB creates index entries per array element automatically; a compound index may only include one array field
- **`explain('executionStats')` confirms index use** — look for `IXSCAN` vs `COLLSCAN` in the winning plan; `totalKeysExamined` vs `nReturned` ratio reveals index efficiency

sections.title: How to Explain MongoDB Index Types
sections.content:
MongoDB's indexing model is similar to relational databases — B-tree for most queries, compound indexes following a left-prefix rule — but with several types specialized for its document model.

**Single-field and compound indexes**
- A single-field index on `{ user_id: 1 }` supports equality and range queries on that field; adding `{ status: 1 }` as a second field creates a compound index — which means `{ user_id: 1, status: 1 }` serves queries filtering on `user_id` alone or both `user_id` and `status`, but not `status` alone
- The left-prefix rule is the same as in SQL: the leading field(s) must appear in the query filter, or MongoDB falls back to a COLLSCAN

**Sparse indexes — index only documents that have the field**
- A sparse index excludes documents where the indexed field is absent or null — `db.users.createIndex({ phone: 1 }, { sparse: true })` only indexes documents that have a `phone` field
- This is useful for optional fields where most documents don't have the field; a non-sparse index would include all those null entries, wasting space and slowing range scans

**TTL indexes — automatic expiry**
- A TTL (Time-To-Live) index on a date field automatically deletes documents after a specified duration — `db.sessions.createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 86400 })` deletes sessions 24 hours after creation
- MongoDB's TTL monitor runs every 60 seconds, so expiry is approximate — documents may persist up to a minute past their TTL; for hard real-time expiry, check the timestamp in the application

**Multikey indexes — for arrays**
- MongoDB automatically creates a multikey index when the indexed field contains an array — `{ tags: 1 }` on a document with `tags: ["java", "spring"]` creates index entries for each element
- A compound index can have at most one array field; indexing two array fields in the same compound index is not allowed

Run `explain('executionStats')` to confirm index usage and check `nReturned` vs `totalKeysExamined` — a large ratio indicates the query is examining far more index entries than it returns, signaling index inefficiency.

questions.question: How does the MongoDB aggregation pipeline work, and how do you use $match, $group, and $lookup stages in a Java application?
questions.title: MongoDB Aggregation Pipeline: $match, $group, $lookup
questions.direct_answer: The aggregation pipeline is a sequence of stages that transform documents as they pass through. $match filters documents (like a WHERE clause), $group aggregates documents by a key and computes accumulators (like GROUP BY + COUNT/SUM), and $lookup performs a left-outer join with another collection. In Spring Boot you compose these stages using the Aggregation fluent API from Spring Data MongoDB or raw BasicDBObject / Document objects via MongoTemplate.
questions.interviewer_intent: Evaluate practical ability to write non-trivial queries beyond simple find(), and check understanding of pipeline ordering and performance implications.

sections.title: Aggregation Pipeline Overview
sections.content:
MongoDB's aggregation framework processes documents through a configurable pipeline of transformation stages. Each stage receives the output of the previous one. The order matters enormously for performance: always place $match and $project stages early to reduce the document set before expensive stages like $group or $lookup. The pipeline runs server-side, making it far more efficient than fetching all documents and aggregating in Java. Spring Data MongoDB wraps the pipeline in a clean Aggregation builder API.

The aggregation pipeline is MongoDB's answer to SQL's GROUP BY, JOINs, and window functions. It processes documents through a sequence of stages, where each stage transforms the document stream and passes results to the next. The order of stages matters for both correctness and performance.

**`$match`** filters documents early — always place it as early as possible to reduce the dataset before expensive operations like `$group` or `$lookup`. When `$match` is the first stage and targets indexed fields, MongoDB uses the index just like a `find()` query.

**`$group`** aggregates documents by a grouping key and applies accumulator expressions: `$sum`, `$avg`, `$push`, `$addToSet`, `$min`, `$max`. The grouping key can be a single field, a combination of fields, or `null` for whole-collection aggregation.

**`$lookup`** performs a left outer join with another collection — the closest equivalent to a SQL JOIN. The `pipeline` variant (introduced in MongoDB 3.6) allows filtering and projecting within the join, avoiding the transfer of entire joined documents.

**`$project` / `$addFields`** reshape documents by including, excluding, or computing new fields. `$addFields` is preferred over `$project` when you want to add fields without explicitly listing all existing ones.

In Spring Data MongoDB, pipelines are built using `Aggregation.newAggregation(matchOp, groupOp, ...)` with type-safe `Criteria` and `Fields` objects, or via `MongoTemplate.aggregate()` with raw `Document` pipelines for full MQL control.

sections.title: Recipe 1 — $match + $group: Count orders per customer in the last 30 days
Recipe 2 — $lookup: Join orders with customer details
Recipe 3 — Raw pipeline with Document (when you need full MQL control)
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`$match` first to reduce document count** — a `$match` as the first stage lets MongoDB use an index to satisfy it; placing it later means all documents are processed before filtering
- **`$group` with accumulators** — `$sum`, `$avg`, `$push`, `$addToSet` are the key accumulators; `_id` is the grouping key — `null` groups all documents into one
- **`$lookup` performs server-side joins** — joins a foreign collection on a field value; result arrives as an array; `$unwind` flattens it for one-to-one lookups; avoid in the hot path of large sharded aggregations
- **`$unwind` followed by `$group` is a re-aggregation pattern** — unwind an embedded array to process each element individually, then re-group to produce a new aggregate
- **Pipeline order determines performance** — reduce cardinality early with `$match` and `$limit`; heavy transformations (`$group`, `$lookup`) should operate on the smallest possible document set

sections.title: How to Explain the Aggregation Pipeline
sections.content:
MongoDB's aggregation pipeline is a sequence of stages where documents flow in at one end and a transformed result comes out the other. Each stage operates on the documents it receives and passes its output to the next — similar to Unix pipes for data.

**$match — filter early**
- `$match` filters documents using the same query syntax as `find()` — `{ $match: { status: "active" } }` passes only active documents to the next stage
- Put `$match` as early as possible in the pipeline — it reduces the number of documents subsequent stages process, and MongoDB can use an index to satisfy the match condition when it's the first stage

**$group — aggregate and compute**
- `$group` collapses documents sharing the same `_id` expression into one, computing accumulated values — `{ $group: { _id: "$customer_id", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } }` gives total revenue per customer
- `$sum`, `$avg`, `$min`, `$max`, `$push` (collect into array), and `$addToSet` (collect unique values) are the common accumulators

**$lookup — server-side join**
- `$lookup` joins documents from another collection — `{ $lookup: { from: "customers", localField: "customer_id", foreignField: "_id", as: "customer" } }` embeds matching customer documents into each order
- The joined field arrives as an array; use `$unwind` to flatten it for cases where exactly one match is expected
- `$lookup` does not use indexes from the foreign collection on sharded clusters; keep the pipeline's input set small with `$match` before `$lookup`

**$project and $addFields**
- `$project` controls which fields appear in output documents — `{ $project: { name: 1, total: 1, _id: 0 } }` keeps only name and total
- `$addFields` adds computed fields without removing existing ones — often combined with `$project` to compute derived values like age from birthdate

Use `$limit` early in the pipeline when you only need a fixed number of results — it reduces the work done by subsequent stages.

questions.question: How do you define custom queries in Spring Data MongoDB repositories, and what are the different query mechanisms available?
questions.title: Spring Data MongoDB Repository Queries
questions.direct_answer: Spring Data MongoDB repositories support four query mechanisms: derived query methods (method name parsed into MQL), @Query annotations with MQL JSON, the Criteria/Query API via MongoTemplate, and the Aggregation API for complex pipelines. Derived methods are best for simple filters; @Query gives you direct MQL control; MongoTemplate is used for programmatic or dynamic queries; and Aggregation handles grouping, joining, and transformation.
questions.interviewer_intent: Check that the candidate knows all the query mechanisms available in Spring Data MongoDB and can select the right one for different complexity levels.

sections.title: Spring Data MongoDB Query Mechanisms Overview
sections.content:
Spring Data MongoDB follows the same repository abstraction as Spring Data JPA. Extend MongoRepository<T, ID> to get basic CRUD for free. Beyond that, Spring Data provides a layered query system: the simplest is derived query methods where the framework parses the method name into a MongoDB query; next is @Query for explicit MQL; then the Criteria + Query + MongoTemplate API for fully programmatic queries; and finally the Aggregation API for multi-stage pipelines. Knowing when to move up the stack is the mark of an experienced developer.

Beyond derived query methods and `@Query`, `MongoTemplate` with `Criteria` objects provides the most flexibility for dynamic queries. The `Criteria` API mirrors MongoDB's query operators: `Criteria.where("price").lt(100).and("category").is("electronics")` builds the equivalent of `{price: {$lt: 100}, category: "electronics"}`. Combined with `Query` objects that add sorting, projection, and pagination, this approach handles complex search forms where filters are conditionally applied at runtime.

For reactive applications, `ReactiveMongoRepository` returns `Flux<T>` and `Mono<T>` instead of `List<T>` and `Optional<T>`, enabling non-blocking I/O through the entire stack. The underlying MongoDB Reactive Streams driver uses Netty for async socket I/O, avoiding thread-per-request blocking.

sections.title: Derived query methods — zero boilerplate for simple filters
sections.content: Spring Data parses the method name to build the query. Use keywords like findBy, countBy, existsBy, deleteBy followed by field names connected with And, Or, Between, In, etc.

sections.title: @Query annotation — write MQL directly on the repository method
sections.content: Use @Query when the derived method name would become unwieldy or when you need MQL operators not expressible through naming conventions.

sections.title: MongoTemplate + Criteria — fully programmatic, dynamic queries
sections.content: When query conditions are only known at runtime (e.g., a search form with optional filters), build a Query object programmatically using the Criteria API.

sections.title: ReactiveMongoRepository — non-blocking queries with Project Reactor
sections.content: For Spring WebFlux applications, swap MongoRepository for ReactiveMongoRepository. All methods return Mono<T> or Flux<T>, enabling end-to-end reactive pipelines.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Derived methods for simple equality and range filters** — `findByStatusAndCreatedAtAfter` generates the query from the method name; no `@Query` annotation needed for straightforward conditions
- **`@Query` for filters derived methods can't express** — `$or`, `$elemMatch`, nested field paths, and complex boolean logic require writing the MongoDB query document directly
- **Criteria API for conditional query building** — add filter conditions only when the corresponding parameter is non-null; avoids generating queries with empty or wildcard conditions
- **`MongoTemplate.aggregate()` for pipeline operations** — repository layer cannot express `$group`, `$lookup`, or multi-stage pipelines; `MongoTemplate` is required for aggregation
- **Projections reduce data transfer** — `@Query(fields = "{'name': 1, 'status': 1}")` or `Query.fields().include("name")` returns only requested fields, reducing network and deserialization overhead for large documents

Spring Data MongoDB provides four levels of query capability — derived methods, `@Query`, Criteria API, and MongoTemplate — and knowing when to step down from the higher-level abstractions to the lower-level ones is what matters in practice.

**Derived query methods — for simple queries**

**`@Query` annotation — for custom queries**

- The Criteria API and repository layer can't express aggregation pipelines — use `mongoTemplate.aggregate()` with an `Aggregation` builder for `$group`, `$lookup`, and multi-stage pipelines

questions.question: How does MongoDB support multi-document ACID transactions, and what are the limitations you should be aware of?
questions.title: MongoDB Transactions (Multi-Document ACID)
questions.direct_answer: Since MongoDB 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters), multi-document ACID transactions are supported. They provide atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability across multiple documents and collections — exactly like SQL transactions. In Spring Boot, you use @Transactional from Spring's transaction abstraction, backed by MongoTransactionManager. Key limitations include: transactions must run on replica sets (not standalone), they carry higher latency than single-document writes, and you should prefer single-document atomicity when possible.
questions.interviewer_intent: Gauge understanding of MongoDB's transaction model, its prerequisites, and when to reach for transactions versus relying on MongoDB's atomic single-document guarantees.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Multi-document transactions since MongoDB 4.0 (replica sets), 4.2 (sharded)** — full ACID semantics with snapshot isolation; every read in the transaction sees the same consistent snapshot
- **`@Transactional` works with Spring Data MongoDB** — Spring manages the session and transaction lifecycle; commit on success, rollback on unchecked exception, same as with JPA
- **Single-document operations are always atomic without a transaction** — updating embedded array elements or multiple fields in one document is atomic natively; only use transactions when atomicity is needed across multiple documents
- **Transactions hold document locks** — concurrent transactions touching the same documents block each other; keep transactions short and avoid long-running operations inside them
- **Transactions on sharded clusters require two-phase commit internally** — MongoDB coordinates across shards automatically; performance cost is higher than on a single replica set; shard key design matters for locality

sections.title: How to Explain MongoDB Transactions
sections.content:
MongoDB has supported multi-document ACID transactions since version 4.0 on replica sets and 4.2 on sharded clusters. They work with snapshot isolation — every read in the transaction sees a consistent snapshot from the moment the transaction started.

**How they work**
- Use `mongoClient.startSession()` and `session.startTransaction()` — all operations in the transaction pass the session object, and MongoDB groups them atomically
- With Spring Data MongoDB and Spring's `@Transactional`, the session management happens automatically — Spring begins the transaction on the session before the method and commits or rolls back when the method exits
- If any operation fails, the entire transaction rolls back and all prior operations in that transaction are undone — the same guarantee as SQL transactions

**When to use them**
- Use multi-document transactions when two or more document writes must be atomic — transferring credits between accounts, deducting inventory while creating an order, updating a user record and its audit log simultaneously
- For single-document operations, MongoDB is always atomic at the document level — updating an embedded array element is atomic without a transaction; transactions add overhead and should be used only when truly needed

**Performance implications**
- Transactions in MongoDB carry overhead — they hold a lock on the documents they modify (similar to row locks in PostgreSQL), which means concurrent transactions touching the same documents block each other
- Long-running transactions increase replication lag because change events are not streamed to secondaries until the transaction commits; keep transactions short
- Transaction timeout defaults to 60 seconds; operations that take longer abort automatically

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Embed for co-accessed, bounded, parent-owned data** — order items belong to one order and are always fetched with it; embedding reads everything in one document access
- **Reference for shared, large, or independently-updated data** — a product referenced by thousands of orders is updated once; embedded in every order, it requires a multi-document update

sections.title: How to Explain Embedding vs Referencing
sections.content:
The single most impactful schema decision in MongoDB is whether to embed related data in a document or reference it with an ID. The rule is: embed when you access the data together; reference when the data is large, shared, or independently updated.

**Embed — when you always read together**
- Embedding puts related data directly in the parent document as a sub-document or array — `order` contains `items: [{ product_id, quantity, price }]` so one document read returns everything needed to display an order
- Embedding is also the right choice when the related data is bounded in size and owned by the parent — comments on a blog post can be embedded if the post has a manageable number of comments, each comment belongs to one post, and comments are never accessed without the post

**Reference — when data is shared or large**
- Referencing stores only the related document's ID and performs a second query (or `$lookup`) to fetch the full data — a product referenced by thousands of orders stores product details once in the `products` collection instead of duplicating them in every order
- Referencing is necessary when the related collection is large (thousands of items per parent), when documents need independent access patterns, or when data is shared across many parents and needs to be updated in one place

**The key questions to drive the decision**
- "Will I ever need this related data without the parent?" — if yes, reference; if the data only makes sense in the context of the parent, embed
- "Does this related data change often?" — if yes and it's embedded in many documents, updating it requires a multi-document update; referencing updates it once
- "How many related items can there be?" — unbounded arrays should be referenced; a document can grow past MongoDB's 16MB limit

The pattern "One-to-Few: embed, One-to-Many: reference, One-to-Squillions: reference" is a useful heuristic from MongoDB's own documentation.

questions.question: How does MongoDB Atlas Search compare to Elasticsearch, and when would you choose one over the other for a Java application?
questions.title: MongoDB Atlas Search vs Elasticsearch
questions.direct_answer: MongoDB Atlas Search is a full-text search engine built directly into MongoDB Atlas, powered by Apache Lucene. Elasticsearch is a standalone, distributed search and analytics engine also built on Lucene. Atlas Search eliminates the need to sync data to a separate cluster, is simpler operationally, and integrates naturally with MongoDB aggregation pipelines. Elasticsearch offers more advanced search features, richer analytics (Kibana), and is better suited to cross-source or high-scale dedicated search workloads.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Atlas Search is Lucene-based, co-located with data** — runs on the same Atlas nodes; no separate cluster to manage; no sync pipeline needed; data is searchable near-immediately after write
- **Elasticsearch provides more control for complex search** — multi-index federation, fine-grained relevance tuning, custom analyzers, and high-volume search throughput at dedicated infrastructure scale
- **Sync to Elasticsearch introduces an eventual consistency window** — dual-write, CDC, or ETL each have failure modes; Atlas Search eliminates this by being in the same system
- **Choose Atlas Search for operational simplicity on Atlas** — if already on Atlas and search requirements are standard (text, fuzzy, autocomplete), Atlas Search avoids an entire separate service
- **PostgreSQL full-text search first for simple cases** — add a dedicated search engine only after validating that the simpler built-in option is insufficient for the actual requirements

sections.title: How to Explain Atlas Search vs Elasticsearch
sections.content:
If you're already on MongoDB Atlas and need full-text search — autocomplete, relevance ranking, faceted navigation — Atlas Search is worth evaluating before adding Elasticsearch as a separate service.

**Atlas Search — built into Atlas, powered by Lucene**
- Atlas Search runs on the same nodes as MongoDB data and uses Apache Lucene under the hood — which means it provides the same text analysis capabilities as Elasticsearch (tokenization, stemming, fuzzy matching, autocomplete) without a separate sync pipeline
- Because it's co-located with the data, there's no eventual consistency lag between writes and search visibility — writes indexed through Atlas Search are typically searchable within a short window, and in some configurations near-immediately

**Elasticsearch — the standalone option**
- Elasticsearch is the industry standard for complex search scenarios: multi-index search, custom relevance tuning, complex aggregation pipelines for analytics, and very high query volumes
- The operational downside: Elasticsearch is a separate cluster to deploy and maintain, and keeping it in sync with the primary database requires a sync strategy — dual writes from the application, CDC via Debezium, or a scheduled ETL job; each has failure modes

**When to choose which**
- Choose Atlas Search when you're already on MongoDB Atlas, the search requirements are straightforward, and you want to avoid a separate sync pipeline; the operational simplicity is the biggest advantage
- Choose Elasticsearch when you have complex relevance requirements, multiple data sources feeding one search index, very high search throughput, or teams with existing Elasticsearch expertise
- Choose neither when PostgreSQL full-text search covers your needs — adding any search service adds operational overhead; validate that simpler tools are insufficient first

questions.question: What are MongoDB change streams and how do you listen to real-time document changes in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Change Streams with Spring Data MongoDB
questions.direct_answer: Change streams allow applications to subscribe to real-time notifications of insert, update, replace, and delete operations on a collection, database, or entire deployment. They are built on the MongoDB oplog and require a replica set or sharded cluster. In Spring Boot you can listen to change streams using the @ChangeStreamListener annotation (Spring Data MongoDB 3.x+), or programmatically via ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream() for a non-blocking reactive pipeline.
questions.interviewer_intent: Test knowledge of event-driven data patterns, how MongoDB surfaces CDC (Change Data Capture) capabilities, and practical Spring Boot integration.

sections.title: Change Streams and Real-Time Events Overview
sections.content:
Change streams are MongoDB's built-in Change Data Capture (CDC) mechanism. Rather than polling a collection for changes, you open a change stream cursor and MongoDB pushes notifications as documents are modified. This is useful for cache invalidation, event-driven microservices, audit trails, and real-time dashboards. Internally, change streams tail the replica set oplog, which means they require a replica set — a standalone instance does not support them. Change streams also support resumable tokens: if your application restarts, it can resume from the last processed event without missing changes.

Change streams use MongoDB's oplog (operations log) as the underlying mechanism. When you open a change stream, the driver tails the oplog and filters events matching your specified collection, database, or deployment scope. This is more efficient than polling because the oplog is a capped collection that MongoDB already maintains for replication.

sections.title: How to Explain Change Streams
sections.content:
Change streams are MongoDB's built-in CDC mechanism — they let your application subscribe to real-time notifications of insert, update, replace, and delete events on a collection without polling.

**How they work**
- Change streams are built on MongoDB's oplog (operations log) — the same replication mechanism that replica sets use to propagate writes; change streams expose a filtered, resumable cursor over that event stream
- Each change event includes the operation type (`insert`, `update`, `delete`), the document ID, and the changed fields — for updates with `updateLookup` configured, the full post-change document is also included

**Spring Data MongoDB integration**
- Spring Data MongoDB provides `ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream()` and `@ChangeStreamOptions` for listening to change events in a reactive pipeline
- With Project Reactor: `mongoTemplate.changeStream("orders", ChangeStreamOptions.empty(), Order.class).doOnNext(event -> process(event.getBody()))` subscribes to all order changes
- Change streams are resumable — each event has a resume token; storing the last processed token allows a restarted consumer to pick up where it left off rather than reprocessing from the beginning

**Use cases**
- Cache invalidation: when a product document changes, publish the change to Redis subscribers to invalidate or update the cached product
- Event-driven microservices: emit domain events (OrderPlaced, InventoryUpdated) directly from database writes without a separate outbox table
- Audit logging: capture every modification to sensitive collections and write them to an audit log without modifying the application code that performs the writes

Change streams require a replica set or sharded cluster — they don't work on standalone mongod instances.

questions.question: How do you diagnose and optimize slow queries in MongoDB using explain() and other performance tools?
questions.title: MongoDB Performance: explain() and Query Optimization
questions.direct_answer: The explain() method returns a query plan that shows whether MongoDB used an index (IXSCAN) or a collection scan (COLLSCAN), the number of documents examined versus returned, and execution time. A high ratio of examined-to-returned documents indicates a missing or suboptimal index. Optimization techniques include adding compound indexes, using covered queries (returning only indexed fields), projecting only needed fields, and avoiding large in-memory sorts. MongoDB Atlas Performance Advisor and the slow query log are additional diagnostic tools.
questions.interviewer_intent: Verify that the candidate can identify performance bottlenecks at the database level and knows the right tools and techniques to diagnose and fix them.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`COLLSCAN` = no index used** — examine all documents; find or create an index on the filter fields; the most urgent optimization signal in the explain output
- **`totalKeysExamined` vs `nReturned` ratio** — a high ratio (examined 50,000, returned 10) means the index returned many false positives; a more selective compound index or a covered query reduces it
- **ESR rule for compound indexes** — Equality fields first, Sort fields second, Range fields last; this ordering maximizes index usage for queries that filter, sort, and range in one query
- **`$match` first in aggregation pipelines** — enables MongoDB to use an index to satisfy the match stage; placed later, all documents flow through earlier stages before filtering
- **`allowDiskUse` for large sorts and aggregations** — the default 100MB memory limit causes aggregation failure on large result sets; set `allowDiskUse: true` for analytics queries that exceed it

sections.title: How to Explain Query Optimization with explain()
sections.content:
When a MongoDB query is slow, `explain('executionStats')` is the first tool to use. It shows whether MongoDB used an index or scanned the collection, how many documents it examined, and how many it returned.

**Reading the execution stats**
- `IXSCAN` in the winning plan means an index was used — look at `totalKeysExamined` vs `nReturned`; if the ratio is high (examined 10,000, returned 10), the index is inefficient for this query pattern
- `COLLSCAN` means no index was used — the database examined every document; the most urgent optimization signal; find or create an appropriate index for the filter fields
- `totalDocsExamined` vs `nReturned` discrepancy signals missing or inefficient index coverage; ideally they should be equal (the index returns exactly the documents that match)

**The compound index decision**
- MongoDB's compound index follows the ESR rule: Equality fields first, Sort fields second, Range fields last — `{ status: 1, createdAt: -1, amount: 1 }` for a query filtering on status, sorting by createdAt descending, and ranging on amount
- The sort field in the index must match the sort direction in the query for MongoDB to use the index for sorting; otherwise a separate sort pass runs in memory

**Aggregation pipeline optimization**
- Place `$match` and `$limit` as early as possible — they reduce the document count for all subsequent stages; a `$match` as the first stage can use an index
- `$sort` on a large dataset without an index sorts in memory and can fail with a 100MB sort limit; add an index that covers the sort fields or increase `allowDiskUse`

Use `db.collection.getIndexes()` to see existing indexes and `db.collection.stats()` to see index sizes — large indexes that aren't being used should be dropped to reduce write overhead.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Embedding means storing related data as a sub-document or array within the parent document, which makes reads fast but can lead to large documents and update anomalies.

Referencing stores related data in a separate collection and links via an ID, similar to a foreign key, keeping documents small but requiring $lookup or application-level joins.

Embed when data is read together, has a 1-to-few cardinality, and is not independently updated. Reference when data is shared across many documents, has 1-to-many or many-to-many relationships, or must be updated independently.

questions.question: How do MongoDB replica sets work, and how do read preferences affect how your Spring Boot application reads data?
questions.title: MongoDB Replica Sets and Read Preferences
questions.direct_answer: A MongoDB replica set is a group of mongod processes that maintain the same data set. One node is elected primary (accepts all writes); the others are secondaries that replicate from the primary's oplog. Read preferences control which node a client reads from: primary (default, always consistent), primaryPreferred, secondary (offload reads but potentially stale data), secondaryPreferred, and nearest (lowest latency). In Spring Boot you configure read preference on the MongoClient or per-operation using ReadPreference.
questions.interviewer_intent: Assess understanding of MongoDB's high availability model, the consistency vs. latency trade-off introduced by reading from secondaries, and practical Spring Boot configuration.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **All writes go to the primary** — secondaries replicate asynchronously; read from a secondary immediately after a write may return stale data
- **`writeConcern: majority` for strong durability** — write acknowledged only after a majority of nodes has applied it; prevents data loss on primary failure at the cost of slightly higher write latency
- **`readPreference: secondary` reduces primary load** — reads distributed across secondaries; replication lag means reads may be stale; appropriate for analytics, reports, or data that can tolerate a small delay
- **Elections take 5-30 seconds** — the replica set is unavailable for writes during election; design applications to retry writes on `NotPrimary` errors rather than treating them as permanent failures
- **`readConcern: majority` for strong read consistency** — reads only return data that has been written to a majority of nodes; prevents reading data that might be rolled back on primary failure

sections.title: How to Explain Replica Sets and Read Preferences
sections.content:
A MongoDB replica set is a group of mongod processes that all contain the same data. One node is the primary and accepts all writes; the others are secondaries that replicate from the primary and can serve reads.

**Replication mechanics**
- The primary writes changes to its oplog (operations log) — secondaries continuously tail the primary's oplog and replay operations to stay synchronized
- Replication is asynchronous by default — a write is acknowledged when it's committed to the primary, before any secondary has applied it; this means a primary failure can lose the most recent writes if they weren't yet replicated
- `writeConcern: { w: "majority" }` requires acknowledgment from a majority of nodes before confirming the write — much stronger durability guarantee at the cost of slightly higher write latency

**Read preferences — where reads go**
- `primary` (default): all reads go to the primary — strong consistency, no stale reads
- `primaryPreferred`: reads go to the primary if available, secondaries if the primary is unavailable
- `secondary`: all reads go to secondaries — reduces primary load but introduces replication lag; a read immediately after a write may return stale data
- `nearest`: reads go to the node with the lowest network latency — useful for globally distributed deployments where a local secondary is much closer than the primary

**Elections and failover**
- If the primary becomes unavailable, the replica set holds an election — the secondary with the most current oplog position becomes the new primary; this typically completes in 5-30 seconds
- During the election window, writes are rejected; configure your application to retry writes that fail with a `NotPrimary` error
